content: 1. Objectively measured sedentary time and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) may have distinct relationships with cardiometabolic health in youth. Excessive sedentary time has been proposed as an independent risk factor for cardiometabolic health, whereas MVPA is positively associated with improved cardiometabolic outcomes. 2. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to evaluate the prospective relationships between objectively measured sedentary time, MVPA, and cardiometabolic health indicators in youth. The databases PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and SPORTDiscus were systematically searched for studies published between January 2000 and April 2018. 3. Studies were included if they objectively measured sedentary time and physical activity and examined their associations with body mass index (BMI), waist circumference, triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein (HDL), insulin, blood pressure, or the clustering of these cardiometabolic risk factors. 4. A total of 30 studies were identified, of which 21 were of high quality. No evidence was found to support an association between sedentary time and cardiometabolic outcomes. The relationship between MVPA and individual cardiometabolic risk factors was inconsistent. 5. The review concluded that there is no prospective association between sedentary time and cardiometabolic health in youth. However, MVPA is beneficially associated with cardiometabolic health in this population. 6. Another systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesize evidence on the relationship between sedentary behaviors (SB) and anxiety symptoms across children, adolescents, and adults. It also examined whether the SB-anxiety relationship is moderated by age group (children/adolescents vs. adults) and participants’ health status (general population vs. individuals with chronic physical or mental illness). 7. A comprehensive search of databases such as PsycINFO, PsycARTICLES, Academic Search Complete, ERIC, Health Source: Nursing/Academic Edition, and MEDLINE identified 31 original studies for the systematic review (total N = 99,192) and 17 studies for the meta-analysis (total N = 27,443). 8. The main inclusion criteria required studies to test the SB-anxiety relationship, achieve a quality score above 65%, and be published in English. The study adhered to the PRISMA guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO. 9. Moderator analyses suggested stronger effects of SB on anxiety among adults compared to children and adolescents. However, further longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the predictive direction of the SB-anxiety relationship and to determine whether the effects depend on the type of anxiety indicators used. 10. A systematic review synthesized evidence on the associations between activity patterns and cardiometabolic risk factors in children and adolescents aged 5–19 years. The review highlighted the need for consensus on defining activity patterns to identify which are most beneficial for cardiometabolic health in youth. 11. From 15,947 articles identified, 29 studies were included in the review. Twenty-four studies were observational (cross-sectional and/or longitudinal), and five were experimental. Ten studies examined physical activity patterns, while 19 focused on sedentary patterns. Only one study investigated both physical activity and sedentary time patterns. 12. Significant variability in the definitions of activity patterns made it challenging to determine which patterns were most beneficial for cardiometabolic health. However, the review identified potential insights and research gaps. 13. Another systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of chronic exercise interventions on executive functions (EFs) in children and adolescents. Chronic exercise was defined as physical activity involving multiple sessions per week over an extended period (typically more than six weeks). 14. Nineteen randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a total of 5,038 participants were included. Chronic exercise interventions, particularly those implemented in curricular or sports settings, showed small but promising effects on various aspects of executive functions, especially inhibitory control. 15. Despite the small effect sizes, chronic exercise interventions may be a viable strategy to enhance executive functions in children and adolescents. Further research is needed to explore the long-term impact of these interventions on cognitive and academic outcomes.
